planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, keeping seed trays in darkness until germination, and transplant out once frost danger has passed.

directions: Casino Mix is a dwarf, well-branched strain of painted tongue bred for bedding and container use, staying under 14 inches while still producing the trumpet-shaped, gold-veined flowers in reds, yellows, purples, and rose that make this genus so striking. Sow seed under cover and keep it dark until germination, since light inhibits sprouting, then grow on cool and bright before hardening off. Set plants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and pinch young growth once to encourage bushier, more floriferous plants. Because it fades quickly in high heat, treat it as a spring and fall display in hot-summer regions.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter climates.

directions: Penny Black is a striking selection of California's baby blue eyes, with velvety near-black petals rimmed in a thin band of white instead of the sky-blue of the species. Sow it directly where it will bloom, since the low, sprawling plants resent transplanting, and keep the seedbed evenly moist until germination. It performs best with morning sun and light afternoon shade in warmer gardens, weaving nicely along border edges or in containers where the dark blooms show off against silver or chartreuse foliage companions. Deadhead spent flowers to extend the bloom window before summer heat ends the display.

planting.note: Sow in fall in mild-winter areas or early spring elsewhere; tolerates sandier, leaner soil than its yellow-flowered relative.

directions: White tidy tips is a wiry, aromatic California and Great Basin native annual bearing white ray flowers with soft yellow centers, distinct from the yellow-and-white blooms of its coastal cousin Layia platyglossa. It is at home in the driest, sandiest, most nutrient-poor soils of desert and inland flats, so avoid rich garden beds or extra fertilizer, which produce lanky, flop-prone plants. Scatter seed on a lightly raked surface in fall and let winter rains do the germinating; established plants need no supplemental water in most years. Combine it with other desert annuals like desert dandelion or bladderpod for a naturalistic dry-garden meadow.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained soil in full sun for a spring bloom; germinates with winter rains.

directions: California gilia produces dense, pincushion-like clusters of pale lavender-blue flowers atop slender, openly branched stems, and it is a common sight in the state's coastal grasslands and oak-woodland openings each spring. Broadcast seed on cleared, lean soil in fall so it can germinate and establish a root system through the cool, wet season ahead of its spring flowering. It needs no irrigation once winter rains taper off and actually performs poorly with extra summer water, which shortens its life and encourages fungal problems. Let a portion of the flower heads mature and shatter in place to keep a colony going year after year.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; plants are low and sprawling.

directions: Evening snow earns its name by holding its white, yellow-throated, funnel-shaped flowers closed through the heat of the day and opening them only as temperatures drop in late afternoon and evening, when their faint fragrance also becomes noticeable. This low, wiry California native scrambles over dry, open slopes and washes, so give it lean, fast-draining soil and avoid crowding it with taller, thirstier neighbors. Sow directly in fall onto bare, undisturbed soil, since the fine seed needs good soil contact and the cool, moist winter period to germinate. It thrives entirely on winter and spring rainfall and should not be watered through summer dormancy.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in mild climates or early spring in colder regions; tolerates disturbed, lean soils.

directions: Large-flowered collomia sends up a single tall, slender, unbranched stem topped by a tight head of tubular, apricot-to-salmon flowers, a color rare among western native annuals and a strong draw for bumblebees and hummingbirds. It ranges from California chaparral and forest edges into the Rocky Mountains, so it tolerates more cold and light shade than most of its Gilia-family relatives, though it still flowers best with several hours of direct sun. Direct sow onto lightly disturbed, well-drained soil, since the seed germinates readily but does not compete well against dense turf or thick mulch. Once established, plants shed seed and readily reappear in gravelly paths, burned areas, and other open disturbed ground.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall; seed germinates best with darkness and cool, moist conditions, so cover lightly.

directions: Whitlavia bears large, deep violet-blue, bell-shaped flowers on upright stems and is closely related to the more sprawling desert bluebells, though it grows taller and more erect and is often found tucked beneath desert shrubs and along washes in Southern California's chaparral and desert transition zones. Cover the seed after sowing, since it germinates best in darkness, and time fall sowing so seedlings establish before winter rains arrive. It needs very little supplemental water and actually resents heavy, poorly drained soil, so a lean, gritty planting site closely mimics its native habitat. Bees work the flowers heavily, making it a good addition to a native pollinator border alongside other spring-blooming Phacelia species.
